question: Move the AED at M.S. 224 Manhattan East School for Arts & Academics into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: M.S. 224 Manhattan East School for Arts & Academics (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "Main Entrance by School Safety; Outside Room 263; 3rd Fl Outside RM 310; 4th Floor Outside 456; 5th fl Outside RM 510".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.48 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 2 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 6 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY EMS Station 10, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 136 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly addresses a documented gap in emergency response. The school's current indoor placement is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year and zero hours in summer [E3], yet the area experiences an expected 1.48 cardiac arrests annually during times when every nearby AED is closed [E4]. This school ranks second among 100 NYC schools for this problem. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5 percent survival versus 43.0 percent without [E7]. The six other AEDs nearby are never open 24/7 [E5], making this the only viable option to close a real access gap in a high-need area.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on incomplete data and overlooks a simpler alternative. Yes, the school ranks second for closures during cardiac arrests [E4], but that 1.48 annual figure is ZIP-code level only—we don't know if those calls actually occurred near this specific building [E9]. The nearby fire station, FDNY EMS Station 10, sits just 136 meters away [E8] and is staffed around the clock, making it a natural 24/7 AED host that avoids cabinet costs and vandalism risks [E9]. Before moving school infrastructure, the city should explore whether Station 10 already has an AED or could host one. The survival benefit is real [E7], but so is the unknown cost and maintenance burden of outdoor cabinets [E9].

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that FDNY EMS Station 10 at 136 meters is worth exploring [E8], but it cannot replace this proposal. We don't know whether Station 10 has an AED, is willing to host one, or would accept public access during response calls—all unknowns [E9]. Meanwhile, the documented problem is concrete: this school ranks second among 100 NYC schools for cardiac arrests occurring when all nearby AEDs are unreachable [E4], and the six surrounding AEDs are never open 24/7 [E5]. A street-wall cabinet at M.S. 224 guarantees 24/7 access to this high-need area regardless of fire station cooperation. The city can pursue both options in parallel, but waiting for Station 10 coordination leaves 1.48 annual arrests unprotected [E4].

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The Advocate makes a fair point about not waiting for Station 10 coordination, but the proposal still asks the school to bear unknown costs and maintenance burdens [E9] for a problem we cannot precisely locate. The 1.48 annual arrests are ZIP-code aggregates; we don't know if they cluster near M.S. 224's street wall or elsewhere in 10029 [E9]. A fire station cabinet avoids school liability entirely. The city should simultaneously request Station 10's AED status and capacity rather than commit school resources first. If Station 10 cannot help, the school cabinet becomes the fallback—not the opening move.

verdict.summary: Strong evidence of access gap (1.48 annual arrests during AED closures, rank 2 of 100 schools) and survival benefit (66.5% vs 43.0%) supports action. However, ZIP-code-level data cannot confirm calls occurred near this building, and FDNY EMS Station 10 (136 m away) offers unexplored alternative avoiding school costs and liability.
verdict.strongestFor: School ranks 2nd among 100 NYC schools for cardiac arrests during AED closure hours [E4]; bystander AED shock associates with 66.5% survival [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual call locations unknown—only ZIP-code data available [E9]. FDNY EMS Station 10 at 136 m is staffed 24/7 and may host AED, avoiding school costs and vandalism risk [E8][E9].
verdict.nextStep: Query FDNY EMS Station 10 for current AED status and willingness to host public-access cabinet before committing school resources.
